title: What is this?
goal: Point to the things around you, tell masculine objects from feminine ones, and understand the difference between "a book" and "the book".
bekal: point to things with *haadhaa* and *haadhihi* — and know when to use which
guess the gender of almost any noun just by looking at its ending

dialogs.title: حِوَار — فِي مَكْتَبَةِ الْجَامِعَةِ
dialogs.intro: Budi and Laila at the campus bookshop. Budi points to things one by one.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: This is a dictionary. An Arabic–Indonesian dictionary.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: This is a magazine. The magazine is new.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: لَا، لَيْسَ هٰذَا كِتَابِي. كِتَابِي هُنَاكَ.
lines.baca: laa, laisa haadhaa kitaabii. kitaabii hunaaka.
lines.id: No, this isn't my book. My book is over there.
lines.literal: no, not this book-my. book-my there.

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Blue. The blue book is on the table.

lines.speaker: بُودِي:
lines.id: And this bag? Is it yours?

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.id: Yes, this is my bag. Thank you!

lines.speaker: لَيْلَى:
lines.text: هٰذَا بَابُ الْمَكْتَبَةِ. اَلْمَكْتَبَةُ كَبِيرَةٌ جِدًّا.
lines.id: It's the library door. The library is very big.
lines.literal: this door the-library. the-library big very.

notes: **هٰذَا or هٰذِهِ — not a free choice.** هٰذَا is for masculine things, هٰذِهِ for feminine ones. And "gender" here has nothing to do with living beings: كِتَاب (book) is masculine, طَاوِلَة (table) is feminine. What decides is the form of the word.

**Guessing is easy: look at the ending.** A word ending in ة is almost always feminine (مَجَلَّة, طَاوِلَة, حَقِيبَة, مَكْتَبَة). A word without ة is almost always masculine (كِتَاب, قَامُوس, بَاب, قَلَم). This simple rule covers about nine words out of ten.

**The alif of هٰذَا is written small.** You'll see هذا (no alif) in newspapers and هٰذَا (with a small alif on top) in textbooks. Both are the same; the sound is still *haadhaa* with a long a. This book uses the full form so you don't shorten it by mistake.

**هٰذَا قَامُوسٌ vs هٰذَا الْقَامُوسُ — two very different things.** The first: "this is a dictionary" — a complete sentence. The second: "this dictionary" — not a sentence but a phrase still waiting for something to be said about it: هٰذَا الْقَامُوسُ جَدِيدٌ ("this dictionary is new"). The only difference is اَلْ, and the meaning changes completely.

**لَيْسَ negates a nominal sentence.** A sentence without a verb can't be negated with لَا. You use لَيْسَ: لَيْسَ هٰذَا كِتَابِي ("this isn't my book"), لَسْتُ طَالِبًا ("I'm not a student"). Negating it with لَا is a very typical beginner's mistake.

**كِتَابِي — possession without a word for "my".** The ending ـِي you already used in اِسْمِي works for every noun: كِتَابِي (my book), حَقِيبَتِي (my bag), بَيْتِي (my house). Notice that the ة of حَقِيبَة turns into ت as soon as an ending is attached: حَقِيبَة → حَقِيبَتِي.

**بَابُ الْمَكْتَبَةِ — idafa, possession between two nouns.** "The door of the library". The rule gets fully unpacked in unit 4, but notice it now: the first word (بَاب) **takes no اَلْ and no tanween**; the second word does.

**اَلْكِتَابُ الْأَزْرَقُ — the adjective takes اَلْ too.** If the noun is definite, its adjective must be definite as well. So not اَلْكِتَابُ أَزْرَقُ but اَلْكِتَابُ الْأَزْرَقُ. This is called "agreement", and it applies to gender, definiteness and number all at once.
**جِدًّا always comes after.** "Very big" = كَبِيرَةٌ جِدًّا, not جِدًّا كَبِيرَةٌ. The order is the reverse of English, so think "big very".

grammars.title: Definite and indefinite — اَلْ and tanween
body: English marks this with separate little words, *a* and *the*. Arabic marks it on the word itself, and marking it is not optional.
after: The iron rule: **one word can never have اَلْ and tanween at the same time.** اَلْكِتَابٌ is wrong and stands out immediately. When in doubt, count: one marker only, never two.
Look at the last row: اَلشَّمْسُ is read *ash-shamsu*, not *al-shamsu*. The letter ش is a "sun letter" — the *l* sound merges into it. You can spot this by the shadda on the letter that follows.

grammars.title: Demonstratives: this and that
after: هٰذَا is used for something near (in your hand, in front of you), ذٰلِكَ for something far (across the room) — exactly like English "this" and "that".

For non-human things in the plural, Arabic uses the **feminine singular**: هٰذِهِ الْكُتُبُ ("these books"), not هٰؤُلَاءِ. You'll meet this surprising rule again and again — non-human plurals are treated as one feminine thing.

blocks.text: A handful of words break the ة rule — annoyingly, very common ones. **Feminine without ة**: شَمْس (sun), نَار (fire), أَرْض (earth, land), يَد (hand), عَيْن (eye), نَفْس (soul), and all names of cities and countries. **Masculine despite ending in ة**: خَلِيفَة (caliph), عَلَّامَة (great scholar) — rare at A1.

blocks.title: A way to learn vocabulary that really works
items: Never memorize just كِتَاب. Memorize **كِتَابٌ جَدِيدٌ** — the noun together with one adjective in the matching gender. That way the gender sticks with no extra effort, and you don't have to remember it as a separate fact.
It also saves you from the next big trap: when the adjective has to become جَدِيدَة, your ear will feel at once that something is wrong if you pair it with كِتَاب.

blocks.text: Colors have their own pattern that doesn't follow the usual ة rule: the masculine has the pattern أَفْعَل, the feminine فَعْلَاء.
The last two colors use the ordinary nisba (ـِيّ) because they come from nouns: بُنّ (coffee beans) and رَمَاد (ash). The pattern is exactly the one you used to form nationalities in unit 2.
Asking about color: مَا لَوْنُ الْكِتَابِ؟ (*maa launul-kitaab* — "what color is the book?"). The answer: اَلْكِتَابُ أَحْمَرُ, or simply أَحْمَرُ.
